The graph engine (src/engine/graph.ts) receives a flat list of KBNode[] from the content pipeline and transforms them into a computed KBGraph with edges, clusters, related nodes, and degree maps. All data shapes are imported from the type system, and the engine is called by the orchestrator during startup. Without this module, nodes would float as disconnected islands and the constellation view would be meaningless.

Edge Construction

buildEdges() iterates every node's connections array plus parent field, producing deduplicated KBEdge objects. Deduplication uses a canonical key (edgeKey(a,b) sorts IDs lexicographically) so A→B and B→A collapse to one edge. Edges come from three sources, each assigned a semantic type defined in the typed edges spec:

  1. Explicit connections — declared in node frontmatter or parsed from #N cross-references in issue bodies by the parser
  2. Parent-child containment — any node with a parent field gets a weighted edge (weight 3 via EDGE_TYPE_WEIGHTS.contains) to its parent, pulling them close in the force layout
  3. Orphan rescue — nodes with zero edges are auto-connected to a same-cluster sibling or the graph hub, preventing unreachable dead-ends

The physics drift bug (fixed in 625f054 and 8cf5034) required killing physics after every DataSet update — without this, nodes would slowly creep across the canvas after stabilization.

export function buildGraph(nodes: KBNode[], clusters: Cluster[]): KBGraph {
  const nodeMap = new Map(nodes.map(n => [n.id, n]));
  const edges = buildEdges(nodes, nodeMap);
  // orphan rescue: connect isolated nodes to cluster siblings or hub
  const related = computeRelated(nodes, edges);
  return { nodes, edges, clusters, related };
}

Weighted Related-Node Ranking

computeRelated() builds a per-node adjacency map carrying the highest edge weight between each pair, then sorts neighbors by weight (descending) with degree as tie-breaker — up to 12 neighbors per node. This ranking was redesigned in #52 so strongly-typed edges (like contains at weight 3) outrank weak high-degree connections. Results populate the HUD connections panel via NodeVisual.

Hub Detection

getHubNodeId() prefers the readme node, then overview, otherwise the highest-degree node. This ensures the landing page is always the most connected node. The application shell calls this to determine the initial route. Changed in commit 5c37867 to default to overview instead of readme.

Cluster Collapse

The cluster collapse feature (#57, #58) collapses all nodes in a cluster into a single summary node, reducing visual clutter. The graph network factory and node renderer cooperate to draw collapsed clusters with a stacked appearance.
nodes.title: Graph Engine

nodes.content:
The graph network factory (src/engine/createGraphNetwork.ts) bridges the abstract KBGraph from the graph engine and the visual vis-network library that renders the interactive constellation. It creates vis-network Network instances, configures physics, and manages the emphasis system that highlights a node's neighborhood when hovered.

Creating a Network

createGraphNetwork() accepts a GraphNetworkOptions object (container element, graph data, theme flag, callbacks) and returns a GraphNetworkResult:

export interface GraphNetworkResult {
  network: Network;
  nodes: DataSet<Record<string, unknown>>;
  edges: DataSet<Record<string, unknown>>;
  setEmphasis: (nodeId: string | null) => void;
}

The factory builds vis-nodes via buildVisNode(), which delegates to the node renderer for custom canvas drawing. Node sizes scale with degree — more connections mean a larger node. Hub nodes (top 8 by degree via computeKeyNodes()) get a 1.5× base size boost, giving visual weight to landing-page nodes like overview.

Physics and Stabilization

The network uses barnesHut gravity with force-directed layout. After stabilization completes, physics is killed to prevent drift. This was a hard-won fix: commits 625f054 and 8cf5034 addressed a bug where nodes slowly crept across the canvas after every DataSet update. The solution: disable physics in the factory configuration and again after emphasis updates.

Emphasis System

setEmphasis(nodeId) highlights a node and its direct neighbors at full opacity while fading everything else. This updates vis-network DataSet objects for both nodes and edges. The HUD triggers emphasis on hover, creating a focus-plus-context effect. Passing null resets all nodes to full opacity.

Edge Styling

Edges render per type using EDGE_TYPE_STYLES from the type system. Different edge types get distinct colors, dash patterns, and arrow styles — implemented as part of #56. This makes it visually obvious whether a connection is containment, reference, or cross-reference.

Position Computation

computeGraphPositions() creates a hidden off-screen vis-network to compute force-directed layout positions without rendering. It calls back with a position map used by the HUD minimap's drawMinimap function. The returned cleanup function destroys the hidden network to prevent memory leaks. The dock value is in the dependency array so positions recompute when the dock orientation changes.
nodes.title: Graph Network

nodes.content:
Knowledge lives in many places. Source code in one repository, issues in another, design decisions in a document, architectural context in a pull request thread, tribal knowledge in someone's head. Each system of record captures a piece of the truth — but the connections between them are invisible. You can find the issue, but not the PR that resolved it, the files it changed, the Wikipedia concept it implements, or the design decision that motivated it.

kbexplorer builds a knowledge graph overlay across these isolated islands of information, making the interconnections between them navigable for both humans and agents.

The interface

See kbexplorer in action: the constellation graph with its multi-tier edge importance, three themes (dark, light, sepia), dock positions that rearrange the entire layout, different node types from GitHub issues to Wikipedia articles, and the card overview for scanning the full knowledge base at a glance.

How it works

kbexplorer connects to multiple node providers — systems of record like GitHub, authored documentation, Wikipedia, organizational charts — and pulls their data into a unified graph. The provider pipeline merges nodes from every source, and the graph engine discovers relationships: inline references, cross-links, shared identities, structural containment. What emerges is a constellation where every node connects to the things that give it meaning.

The GitHub provider brings in issues, pull requests, source trees, and commit history. The authored provider processes markdown content with YAML frontmatter. External providers reach beyond the repo — Wikipedia articles for conceptual grounding, organizational charts for team structure, or any data source you wire up.

Three ways to explore

The constellation graph is the signature view — a force-directed visualization where nodes cluster by theme and edges reveal relationships across systems of record. Follow an edge from a design decision to the PR that implemented it to the source files it changed.

The reading view is for depth. Click any node and its full content unfolds — rendered with inline links that connect you to every other node it touches. Related nodes appear in the sidebar. You're never more than one click from context.

The card overview is for breadth. Every node as a card, grouped by cluster, scannable at a glance. When you need to answer "what's in this knowledge base?" — start here.

Why a graph overlay

The value isn't in any single system of record — it's in the connections between them. An issue references a file. A PR closes that issue and modifies three modules. A Wikipedia article explains the algorithm those modules implement. A design decision document captures why that algorithm was chosen over alternatives.

These relationships exist, but they're scattered across tools that don't talk to each other. kbexplorer surfaces them as typed, weighted edges in a navigable graph. The HUD gives you layer toggles, cluster collapse, a detail slider, and multi-tier edge importance that fades distant connections while keeping your neighborhood sharp.

kbexplorer enforces graph constraints: no orphan nodes, every node within three hops of the hub, edges typed and weighted so the constellation is a legible map — not a hairball.

Start exploring

Pick a cluster chip above, click into a curated node, or open the constellation and follow the edges. The graph is yours to explore.

nodes.content:
The HUD (src/components/HUD.tsx) is the persistent sidebar that provides orientation and navigation throughout kbexplorer. It contains the minimap constellation, related node panels, layer toggles, cluster collapse controls, and docking options. It is always visible regardless of which view is active — this is what makes it a heads-up display rather than a simple sidebar.

Minimap

The minimap renders a small-scale version of the full constellation using a <canvas> element. The drawMinimap function reads positions from computeGraphPositions() in the graph network module and draws nodes as colored dots. The current node is highlighted, giving spatial context for where you are in the graph. The minimap uses one canvas ref per dock orientation (vertical vs horizontal) — when the dock switches, the canvas unmounts and remounts, and the draw effect re-fires via dock in the dependency array.

Layer Toggles

Added in #55 as part of the sense-making epic (#54), layer toggles show/hide groups of node types: Content (authored), File (source), Work (issues/PRs), and Concept. This filters the graph without changing the underlying data — nodes are hidden at the vis-network level.

Cluster Collapse

Clicking a cluster label collapses all its nodes into a single summary node (#57, #58). The node renderer draws collapsed clusters with a stacked appearance. This dramatically reduces visual clutter for large clusters.

Related Panel

The related panel shows up to 12 neighboring nodes for the currently selected node, rendered as NodeVisual cards. The ranking weights edge type then degree — strongly-typed edges (like contains) outrank weak links, as redesigned in #52.

Dock Positions

The HUD can dock to left, right, bottom, or top. Dock position persists in localStorage. The dock rework in PR #28 added depth controls and overlay animation alongside the docking system. The style system provides the CSS for each dock variant.

Neighborhood View

The active node neighborhood view (#59) filters the minimap to show only the N-hop neighborhood of the focused node, reducing information overload in dense graphs.

<HUD graph={graph} activeNodeId={currentId} onNodeClick={navigateToNode} dock={dockPosition} />

The application shell renders the HUD at the top level so it persists across view transitions.

nodes.content:
The identity system (src/engine/identity.ts) solves a fundamental problem: the same real-world entity — a source file, a component, a concept — can appear as multiple nodes produced by different providers. Without stable identities, the graph engine would treat urn:file:src/engine/graph.ts from the files provider and the authored graph-engine content node as completely unrelated things.

How Identity Works

Each KBNode receives an identity field — a URN string generated by assignIdentity() based on the node's source.type. The function is a simple switch that maps source types to URN namespaces:

export function assignIdentity(node: KBNode): string | undefined {
  switch (node.source.type) {
    case 'file':         return `urn:file:${node.source.path}`;
    case 'authored':     return `urn:content:${node.id}`;
    case 'readme':       return 'urn:content:readme';
    case 'issue':        return `urn:issue:${node.source.number}`;
    case 'pull_request': return `urn:pr:${node.source.number}`;
    case 'commit':       return `urn:commit:${node.source.sha}`;
    case 'section':      return undefined; // sections don't get identities
  }
}

Section nodes intentionally return undefined — they are sub-parts of a parent and don't represent independent entities.

Identity Matching

shareIdentity(a, b) checks whether two nodes represent the same entity by comparing their URN strings. This is used by the view system to merge representations — if a file node and a content node share an identity, the graph can display them as facets of the same concept. The full design rationale is in the multi-layer identity spec, implemented in #47 alongside the provider system (commit 930f94c).

The Identity Index

buildIdentityIndex() creates a Map<string, string[]> from URN to all node IDs sharing that identity. This enables the parser to merge information from different sources and the view system to cross-reference layers.

Why URNs

URNs were chosen because file paths change during refactoring, issue numbers are repo-specific, and content IDs are arbitrary. URNs provide a stable, namespaced identifier that survives restructuring. The file: field in nodemap.yaml entries creates identity links between authored content and source files — see the node mapping system. The Visual Identity System (#9) ensures these identities render consistently across all seven display surfaces.

Integration Points

The identity system is called by:

  • The parser during parseMarkdownFile() — sets identity on authored nodes
  • The authored provider — ensures urn:content: prefix
  • The files provider — assigns urn:file: identities
  • The work provider — assigns urn:issue: and urn:pr: identities
  • The local loader — identity assignment for manifest-loaded nodes

All URN formats are defined in the type system and documented in the multi-layer identity spec.
nodes.title: Identity System

nodes.content:
The inline link extraction specification defines the principle that inline links ARE the graph edges. Rather than requiring authors to maintain a separate connections array in frontmatter, the system extracts edges directly from the markdown content — every [text](target) link that resolves to a known node ID becomes an edge.

Core Principle

A markdown link [Graph Engine](graph-engine) does double duty:

  1. It renders as a clickable link in the reading view
  2. It creates a references edge in the graph engine with source inferred

This was designed in #48 and implemented in commit 472396c.

How Extraction Works

The parser's parseMarkdownFile() scans the body for inline links, filtering out external URLs (http), anchors (#), and image paths (.png, .jpg). Remaining targets are matched against known node IDs. Commit 941e9be added file-path reference extraction, and 79fc1e0 extended it to README content.

// Links extracted from markdown body
[Graph Engine](graph-engine)     → edge to graph-engine
[src/types](type-system)         → edge to type-system

Why This Matters

Without inline link extraction, content authors would maintain both prose links and frontmatter connection arrays — a duplication that always drifts out of sync. By deriving edges from content, the graph stays accurate as long as the prose is accurate. The typed edges spec categorizes these as references type with inferred source.

Clickable File References

Issue #51 extended this to file path references — when content mentions src/engine/parser.ts, the edge exists in graph data, but originally rendered as a plain <code> tag. The fix made paths clickable in the reading view.

Integration

The extraction runs during parsing in the parser, feeding edges to the graph engine. The design decisions and content pipeline nodes cover the broader context.

Content from GitHub API

Data Sources

  • Fetches issues, README, and the full file tree from the GitHub API
  • PRs and commits are not fetched — removed due to unreliable linking between PR nodes and the rest of the graph

File Tree Processing

  • Generates a repo-root node, directory nodes (2 levels deep), and individual source file nodes for .ts, .tsx, .md, .json, .yaml, and .css files
  • Each file node is parented to its containing directory node

README Handling

  • README content is decoded with TextDecoder instead of atob to fix UTF-8 encoding issues with base64 content
  • Content-based connections are created via keyword matching: a connection forms when 60% or more of a target node's title words appear in the README body
  • #N issue references in the README also generate explicit connections

Issue Processing

  • Issues with 2 or more headings are split into a parent node plus individual section nodes

Caching & Error Handling

  • CACHE_VERSION constant enables cache versioning; stale data is auto-cleared on version bump
  • An error screen is displayed when 0 nodes load (typically due to API rate limiting)

Hub Node Selection

  • The hub node (center of the graph) prefers the readme node; falls back to the highest-degree node

### File Tree Processing
- Generates a **repo-root** node, **directory** nodes (2 levels deep), and individual **source file** nodes for `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.md`, `.json`, `.yaml`, and `.css` files
- Each file node is parented to its containing directory node

### README Handling
- README content is decoded with `TextDecoder` instead of `atob` to fix UTF-8 encoding issues with base64 content
- Content-based connections are created via keyword matching: a connection forms when 60% or more of a target node's title words appear in the README body
- `#N` issue references in the README also generate explicit connections

### Issue Processing
- Issues with 2 or more headings are split into a **parent** node plus individual **section** nodes

### Caching & Error Handling
- `CACHE_VERSION` constant enables cache versioning; stale data is auto-cleared on version bump
- An error screen is displayed when 0 nodes load (typically due to API rate limiting)

### Hub Node Selection
- The hub node (center of the graph) prefers the `readme` node; falls back to the highest-degree node

Vision

Phase 2 introduces an embedded GitHub Copilot conversation panel directly inside kbexplorer. Users will be able to ask questions about the knowledge base — "What issues are related to authentication?", "Summarize the architecture decisions", "What's blocking the next release?" — and receive contextual answers grounded in the loaded graph data.

How It Would Work

  1. A collapsible chat panel slides in from the right side of the reading view, hosted inside a Fluent Dialog component for consistent overlay behavior
  2. The conversation context includes the current node's content, its connections, and the full graph structure
  3. Copilot generates responses using the knowledge graph as grounding — not generic answers, but answers specific to this repository's issues and structure
  4. Responses can include clickable node references that navigate within kbexplorer

Integration Points

  • The HUD (#11) would gain a chat toggle Fluent Button in the right panel
  • The graph view (#10) could support "find nodes about X" queries that highlight matching nodes
  • The reading view would show inline suggestions for related content based on what you're reading
  • The overview could offer a "summarize this cluster" action per cluster group
  • All conversation UI would use Fluent components (Card, Button, Input, Body1, etc.) to match the existing design system

Technical Approach

This would use the GitHub Copilot Extensions SDK to embed a Copilot-powered experience. The knowledge graph (#12) provides structured context that makes responses significantly more relevant than raw repository search. The Fluent theme system (#13) would style the chat panel automatically through FluentProvider context.

This is a Phase 2 feature — the current Phase 1 focuses on making the exploration experience excellent on its own (#9, #10, #11).

nodes.title: Scope boundaries

nodes.content: On real content, a Person node and a Squad node render via bespoke viewers, an arbitrary structured file renders via the generic fallback, and a .github workflow appears as a node edged to the repository node — all without editing core unions to introduce a new kind.

nodes.title: Success definition

nodes.content:
Replace kbexplorer-template's closed, compile-time node-type system — hardcoded NodeSource / DisplayMode / EdgeType unions, a renderContent switch, and bespoke per-source providers — with an open, data-driven one:

  • JSON-LD node internals (@id / @type / typed data) on KBNode.
  • A node-type registry that declares each type's discovery, mapping, cluster, layer, relations, and viewer in one place.
  • A viewer registry keyed by @type with a generic structured fallback (total coverage; bespoke viewers are additive).
  • Schema-driven content-model ingestion that builds the graph from entity files (the model documented in content-model.md).
  • Repo-structural discovery: .github workflows, Actions, and templates become nodes linked to the repository node.
nodes.rawContent:
Replace kbexplorer-template's **closed, compile-time** node-type system — hardcoded `NodeSource` / `DisplayMode` / `EdgeType` unions, a `renderContent` switch, and bespoke per-source providers — with an **open, data-driven** one:

- **JSON-LD node internals** (`@id` / `@type` / typed `data`) on `KBNode`.
- A **node-type registry** that declares each type's discovery, mapping, cluster, layer, relations, and viewer in one place.
- A **viewer registry keyed by `@type`** with a generic structured fallback (total coverage; bespoke viewers are additive).
- **Schema-driven content-model ingestion** that builds the graph from entity files (the model documented in `content-model.md`).
- **Repo-structural discovery**: `.github` workflows, Actions, and templates become nodes linked to the repository node.
nodes.title: What

nodes.content: The originating content-model repo (Xbox Personalization) is being sunset. kbexplorer-template must become the new system of record and own the files→graph pipeline itself — no dependency on an externally pre-built graph.json. Migration will surface new node kinds (squad/cell/crew, sprint/cycle/season, …) that must be absorbed by configuration, not core surgery. Repo structure should be first-class graph citizens. JSON-LD + a viewer registry is the smallest durable abstraction that delivers the originally requested Person / Squad / Team views and scales to arbitrary structured knowledge.

Created: Apr 4, 2026 · Updated: Apr 10, 2026

View on GitHub ↗

Overview

While the default experience uses GitHub API data (#12), kbexplorer also supports an authored mode where content comes from a collection of Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. This mode is designed for curated knowledge bases — design systems, architecture decision records, learning curricula, or team wikis.

Frontmatter Schema

Each .md file declares its metadata in YAML frontmatter:

`yaml

title: Authentication Architecture cluster: security emoji: 🔐 sprite: /images/auth-icon.png hero: /images/auth-hero.jpg connections:

  • id: session-management type: references
  • id: oauth-flow type: depends-on tags: [architecture, security, phase-1]

`

The engine parses these files using gray-matter, builds the graph from explicit connections arrays, and assigns visuals based on the mode selected (#9).

Rendering

All prose is rendered using Fluent tokens for typography and colors. The default font is Segoe UI (via tokens.fontFamilyBase) for body text and headings. Code blocks use Cascadia Code (via tokens.fontFamilyMonospace). Colors, spacing, and radii all come from Fluent tokens through makeStyles — no custom CSS variables or hardcoded values.

Clustering

In authored mode, clusters come from the cluster field rather than GitHub labels. This gives authors explicit control over how nodes group in the overview grid and the constellation graph (#10). The same cluster colors and visual indicators carry through the HUD (#11) and reading view connections sidebar.

When to Use Which Mode

  • Repo-aware (default): Zero-config exploration of any GitHub repo. Great for project onboarding. PRs are filtered out — only issues, README, and directory structure become nodes.
  • Authored: Curated, designed knowledge experiences. Requires content creation but offers full control over structure, visuals, and narrative flow.

## Overview

While the default experience uses GitHub API data (#12), kbexplorer also supports an **authored mode** where content comes from a collection of Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. This mode is designed for curated knowledge bases — design systems, architecture decision records, learning curricula, or team wikis.

### Frontmatter Schema

Each `.md` file declares its metadata in YAML frontmatter:

`yaml
---
title: Authentication Architecture
cluster: security
emoji: 🔐
sprite: /images/auth-icon.png
hero: /images/auth-hero.jpg
connections:
  - id: session-management
    type: references
  - id: oauth-flow
    type: depends-on
tags: [architecture, security, phase-1]
---
`

The engine parses these files using `gray-matter`, builds the graph from explicit `connections` arrays, and assigns visuals based on the mode selected (#9).

### Rendering

All prose is rendered using Fluent tokens for typography and colors. The default font is **Segoe UI** (via `tokens.fontFamilyBase`) for body text and headings. Code blocks use **Cascadia Code** (via `tokens.fontFamilyMonospace`). Colors, spacing, and radii all come from Fluent tokens through `makeStyles` — no custom CSS variables or hardcoded values.

### Clustering

In authored mode, clusters come from the `cluster` field rather than GitHub labels. This gives authors explicit control over how nodes group in the overview grid and the constellation graph (#10). The same cluster colors and visual indicators carry through the HUD (#11) and reading view connections sidebar.

### When to Use Which Mode

- **Repo-aware** (default): Zero-config exploration of any GitHub repo. Great for project onboarding. PRs are filtered out — only issues, README, and directory structure become nodes.
- **Authored**: Curated, designed knowledge experiences. Requires content creation but offers full control over structure, visuals, and narrative flow.

nodes.title: scripts/generate-manifest.js ignores VITE_KB_HOST_ROOT in vendored installs

nodes.content:
detectHostRoot() resolves kbRoot/../.., which only works for git-submodule layouts (where .kbexplorer is two levels deep). In vendored mode that path lands above the host repo, the lookup fails, and the script falls back to treating kbRoot as the host.

The companion CLI (anokye-labs/kbexplorer-cli) already passes VITE_KB_HOST_ROOT=<host> via env on dev/build, but this script never reads it.
nodes.rawContent:
`detectHostRoot()` resolves `kbRoot/../..`, which only works for git-submodule layouts (where `.kbexplorer` is two levels deep). In vendored mode that path lands **above** the host repo, the lookup fails, and the script falls back to treating `kbRoot` as the host.

The companion CLI (`anokye-labs/kbexplorer-cli`) already passes `VITE_KB_HOST_ROOT=<host>` via env on dev/build, but this script never reads it.
nodes.title: Cause

nodes.content: Until this is fixed, kbexplorer dev in a vendored install renders the template's own knowledge base instead of the user's. Discovered while dogfooding kbexplorer on the CLI repo itself.
nodes.rawContent: Until this is fixed, `kbexplorer dev` in a vendored install renders the template's own knowledge base instead of the user's. Discovered while dogfooding kbexplorer on the CLI repo itself.
nodes.title: Impact

nodes.content:
In a host repo using kbexplorer init --vendor (so .kbexplorer/ lives one level deep inside the host, not as a git submodule):

node .kbexplorer/scripts/generate-manifest.js

writes a manifest containing the template's stock content (37 files starting with content/app-shell.md, README # kbexplorer-template) rather than the host repo's authored content.
nodes.rawContent:
In a host repo using `kbexplorer init --vendor` (so `.kbexplorer/` lives one level deep inside the host, not as a git submodule):

`
node .kbexplorer/scripts/generate-manifest.js
`

writes a manifest containing the **template's stock content** (37 files starting with `content/app-shell.md`, README `# kbexplorer-template`) rather than the host repo's authored content.
nodes.title: Repro

nodes.content:
At the top of the script:

js const hostRoot = process.env.VITE_KB_HOST_ROOT ? resolve(process.env.VITE_KB_HOST_ROOT) : detectHostRoot();

Falls back to existing behavior for standalone use; honors the explicit env var when the CLI provides it.
nodes.rawContent:
At the top of the script:

`js
const hostRoot = process.env.VITE_KB_HOST_ROOT
  ? resolve(process.env.VITE_KB_HOST_ROOT)
  : detectHostRoot();
`

Falls back to existing behavior for standalone use; honors the explicit env var when the CLI provides it.

nodes.title: Epic: Work-graph vocabulary — teams, workstreams, priorities, releases, people

nodes.content: Drop team.yaml / workstream.yaml / release data into a repo and the graph grows an organizational layer: a workstream node links to its priority, its team, its active PRs and issues, its releases; a person node aggregates their authored/assigned work. Resource-first navigation works across it (click a teammate → their workstream → its open PRs).

Resource-first navigation works across it (click a teammate → their workstream → its open PRs).
nodes.title: Outcome

nodes.content:
1. Work-graph entity schema — YAML descriptor shapes for team, workstream, priority, person, system-of-record in the content-model engine, with derived edges (member-of, owns, prioritized-as, tracked-in).
  2. Release nodes — ingestion in kbexplorer-cli (gh release list → manifest) + release node type + edges to PRs/tags here.
  3. Person nodes — promote people from author/assignee strings to first-class nodes aggregating their active work, optionally enriched by the existing OrgChart provider.

Design constraint: schema-first. The descriptor shapes must be reviewable by humans, enforceable in the host repo, and stable across template upgrades (coordinate with kbexplorer-cli#42 capability/protocol work).

2. **Release nodes** — ingestion in kbexplorer-cli (`gh release list` → manifest) + release node type + edges to PRs/tags here.

Design constraint: schema-first. The descriptor shapes must be reviewable by humans, enforceable in the host repo, and stable across template upgrades (coordinate with kbexplorer-cli#42 capability/protocol work).
nodes.title: Scope (sub-issues)

nodes.content:
The target deployment is a work repository where people need sensemaking over active PRs, work items, releases, workstreams, priorities, and what coworkers are doing. Issues/PRs/commits/branches already ingest, but the organizational layer — the thing that turns repo activity into a navigable map of work — has no vocabulary: no team, workstream, priority, release, person, or system-of-record node types.

The F2 content-model pipeline (schema-driven YAML/JSON entity files under content-model/, Epic #147) is exactly the right substrate. The host work repo will enforce consistency with YAML descriptor files; those descriptors ARE the contract this epic defines.

3. **Remediation wave 1** — issues filed from the first assessment, worked through the normal pipeline.

The standard then becomes a recurring gate: future UI PRs cite it, and periodic re-assessment keeps drift visible.
nodes.title: Scope (sub-issues)

nodes.content:
kbexplorer's structural quality has gates (graph validation, assessment scoring, link health). Its experiential quality has none — nothing assesses whether the thing is beautiful: typography rhythm, color and contrast across themes, motion, graph readability, information hierarchy, the feel of moving resource-to-resource. For a sensemaking tool, beauty is not cosmetic; it is load-bearing — visual clarity IS comprehension.

This epic establishes a standard of beauty: an explicit, opinionated quality bar, an agentic review process that assesses the real rendered product against it (screenshots, not source), and a stream of driven improvements.

nodes.title: Epic: Comprehensive testing system — DTU spine across CLI, app, and visual surfaces

nodes.content:
1. CLI ↔ DTU seam [cli] — configurable GitHub API base/auth so the CLI fetches from the Gitea adapter (hermetic) AND a GHE host (real enterprise). Keystone; unblocks the dress rehearsal (cli #56) and the real deployment.
  2. Full-loop deployment scenario — actor mutates twin → CLI regenerates manifest from twin → app renders it → verify reflects the mutation. The end-to-end the real deployment IS.
  3. Work-graph DTU scenarios — actor edits team.yaml/workstream.yaml or cuts a release → app reflects the new team/release node on refresh (extends issue-lifecycle/pr-and-merge to the org layer shipped in #232).
  4. Agent-runtime twin [cli] — deterministic fake agent CLI so derive/generate fuzzy paths run hermetically in full-pipeline tests, not just unit injection.
  5. MCP server twins [cli] — fake ADO board + SharePoint-docs MCP servers so MCP-preflight + derive against work-item/doc sources are exercised hermetically (the work-repo deployment's real dependencies).
  6. Visual-regression gate — wire capture-review + BEAUTY.md into a baseline-diff check (per theme × surface), tied to twin states; catch visual regressions.
  7. TESTING.md — the pyramid + CI orchestration — formalize what runs on PR (unit + static-twin fast gate) vs nightly (live DTU + full-loop + visual) vs exploratory; codify the holdout discipline across all twins.
  8. Exploratory-agent harness — formalize the playbook: a scheduled/triggerable job that launches agent sessions against a running DTU to probe edge cases and open spec PRs (human-reviewed; assertions in specs, never in twins).

CLI-side layers (1, 4, 5) are tracked as issues in anokye-labs/kbexplorer-cli and linked here.

nodes.title: The matrix (service × surface)

nodes.content:
The DTU foundation is live on main: a static GitHub fixture twin (twins/github/, the fast PR gate) and a stateful Gitea live twin (twins/gitea/, Podman + GitHub→Gitea proxy on VITE_GH_API_BASE, scripted actors, nightly). DTU.md states the ambition: local behavioral clones of every external service, with the holdout rule (specs are the holdout set; never code to them).

Today that spine only validates the app (browser, remote mode). The CLI pipeline (init/generate/derive/manifest/build) shells out to gh directly and is tested only by unit injection + the static mock — never against the live, mutating twin. There is no full-loop test (twin mutates → CLI regenerates → app renders → verify), and the project's other external dependencies — agent runtimes (copilot/claude) and MCP servers (ADO, SharePoint) — have no twins at all, despite being the backbone of the local-first regeneration the work-repo deployment depends on.

Those nodes only appear in local-manifest mode (the CLI writes them into the manifest).

Impact: a runtime-mode deployment (app fetching live from GitHub in-browser, no CLI-built manifest) shows issues/PRs/releases but NOT the organizational layer. Two .fixme specs in e2e/gitea/workgraph-mutations.spec.ts document this and can be un-fixme'd when the remote fetch path lands.

So the full-loop never executes in CI, and regressions in the actor→twin→CLI-regen→app-render→verify path would not be caught nightly.

Options

  1. Extend dtu-gitea.yml to also run npm run test:e2e:full-loop after the gitea suite (shares the Podman bringup; cheapest).
  2. Add a dedicated nightly workflow for the full-loop.

Option 1 is likely simplest since the substrate/bringup overlaps. Note the full-loop's default substrate is static (FULL_LOOP_SUBSTRATE=static); the live-Gitea substrate is still deferred, so wiring it nightly may also be a good moment to wire the gitea substrate.

TESTING.md documents this as "tracked separately" and points here.

nodes.content:
• npm run dev loads with zero GitHub API calls in local mode

nodes.title: Acceptance Criteria

nodes.content: kbexplorer fetches ALL content via GitHub API at runtime — authored markdown, file tree, README, issues, PRs, commits, and config.yaml. This causes rate limiting (60 req/hr unauthenticated) and is wasteful for self-exploration where content is on disk.

nodes.title: Problem

nodes.content:
A pre-build script generates a single src/generated/repo-manifest.json containing:

  • Authored content: markdown files from content/ read from disk
  • Config: config.yaml parsed from disk
  • File tree: local file system walk
  • README: read from disk
  • Issues, PRs, commits: fetched via gh CLI at build time (best-effort)

The app imports this manifest in local mode — zero API calls at runtime. Remote mode (GitHub API) is preserved for deployed instances exploring other repos.

nodes.title: Epic: Decouple kbexplorer subsystems & enable pluggable providers/representations

nodes.content:
• Shared contracts live in a separate repo/package @anokye-labs/kbexplorer-core.
  • Affordances are per-retrieval and situational (see §4A of the plan): a source declares a possible universe; each retrieved resource carries the affordances allowed now + hypermedia links. Staging area is a first-class linked resource. Git ≠ GitHub.
  • Provider loading is local-ES-module-first, then 3rd-party npm.
  • llm-context representation is neighbor-anchored & navigable — never the whole graph.
  • Each phase keeps graph output byte-identical until a seam is intentionally flipped.
nodes.rawContent:
- Shared contracts live in a **separate repo/package** `@anokye-labs/kbexplorer-core`.
- **Affordances are per-*retrieval* and situational** (see §4A of the plan): a source
  declares a possible universe; each retrieved resource carries the affordances allowed
  *now* + hypermedia links. Staging area is a first-class linked resource. **Git ≠ GitHub.**
- Provider loading is **local-ES-module-first**, then 3rd-party npm.
- `llm-context` representation is **neighbor-anchored & navigable** — never the whole graph.
- Each phase keeps graph output **byte-identical** until a seam is intentionally flipped.

nodes.title: Success definition

nodes.content: Today the three subsystems — system-of-record + providers, the resource-graph-engine, and the representation/rendering subsystem — are entangled: two fat loaders duplicate ~150 lines of post-processing, there is no first-class system-of-record abstraction, 3rd-party providers cannot actually load (hardcoded plugin switch), representation styling is baked into core data types, and the SPA is the only output format. Target: a clean 4-layer pipeline — Sources → Providers → Engine (pure KBGraph) → Representation registry — backed by a shared @anokye-labs/kbexplorer-core contracts package, so authors can bring their own local or 3rd-party providers, sources, and representations without forking core.
nodes.rawContent:
Today the three subsystems — system-of-record + providers, the resource-graph-engine,
and the representation/rendering subsystem — are entangled: two fat loaders duplicate
~150 lines of post-processing, there is no first-class system-of-record abstraction,
3rd-party providers cannot actually load (hardcoded plugin switch), representation
styling is baked into core data types, and the SPA is the only output format. Target: a
clean 4-layer pipeline — **Sources → Providers → Engine (pure `KBGraph`) → Representation
registry** — backed by a shared `@anokye-labs/kbexplorer-core` contracts package, so
authors can bring their own local or 3rd-party providers, sources, and representations
without forking core.

nodes.title: Requirements

nodes.content:
• Walks local file system → produces GHTreeItem-compatible tree (filters dotfiles/node_modules/dist)
  • Reads README.md from disk
  • Reads content/*.md files → embeds raw markdown keyed by path
  • Reads config.yaml → parses and embeds
  • Fetches issues via gh issue list --json ... --state all --limit 200 (best-effort)
  • Fetches PRs via gh pr list --json ... --state all --limit 200 (best-effort)
  • Fetches commits via git log or gh api (best-effort, last 50)
  • Host-aware: detects submodule mode and reads from host repo root
nodes.rawContent:
- Walks local file system → produces GHTreeItem-compatible tree (filters dotfiles/node_modules/dist)
- Reads `README.md` from disk
- Reads `content/*.md` files → embeds raw markdown keyed by path
- Reads `config.yaml` → parses and embeds
- Fetches issues via `gh issue list --json ... --state all --limit 200` (best-effort)
- Fetches PRs via `gh pr list --json ... --state all --limit 200` (best-effort)
- Fetches commits via `git log` or `gh api` (best-effort, last 50)
- Host-aware: detects submodule mode and reads from host repo root

nodes.title: Feature: Phase 4 — Source abstraction with per-retrieval situational affordances

nodes.content:
One loadKnowledgeBase(source, config) replaces both loaders; goldens byte-identical; a staged file resource carries a staging-area link.

Blocked by: F3.
nodes.rawContent:
One `loadKnowledgeBase(source, config)` replaces both loaders; goldens byte-identical; a
staged file resource carries a `staging-area` link.

**Blocked by:** F3.
nodes.title: Acceptance

nodes.content: Source/Resource/Affordance/Link impls, ManifestSource + GitHubApiSource, provider refactor, single loadKnowledgeBase. Out: write/stage mutations beyond the contract + staging-area linking (kept minimal/read-first).
nodes.rawContent:
`Source`/`Resource`/`Affordance`/`Link` impls, `ManifestSource` + `GitHubApiSource`,
provider refactor, single `loadKnowledgeBase`. Out: write/stage *mutations* beyond the
contract + staging-area linking (kept minimal/read-first).
nodes.title: Scope

nodes.content: Introduce the Source abstraction (§4A): a source declares a possible universe of affordances per kind, but each retrieved resource carries the affordances allowed now plus hypermedia links. Staging area is a first-class linked resource. Git ≠ GitHub — GitHubApiSource is a composite exposing Git resources (file/tree/commit/ staging-area) and GitHub resources (issue/pull-request/release). Refactor providers to consume a Source, and collapse the two loaders into one loadKnowledgeBase(source, config).
nodes.rawContent:
Introduce the `Source` abstraction (§4A): a source declares a *possible universe* of
affordances per kind, but each **retrieved resource carries the affordances allowed *now***
plus hypermedia `links`. Staging area is a first-class linked resource. **Git ≠ GitHub** —
`GitHubApiSource` is a composite exposing Git resources (`file`/`tree`/`commit`/
`staging-area`) and GitHub resources (`issue`/`pull-request`/`release`). Refactor providers
to consume a `Source`, and collapse the two loaders into one `loadKnowledgeBase(source, config)`.
nodes.title: What

nodes.content: No first-class system-of-record today; this is what makes "bring your own SoR" possible and unifies build-time vs runtime wiring.
nodes.rawContent:
No first-class system-of-record today; this is what makes "bring your own SoR" possible
and unifies build-time vs runtime wiring.

nodes.title: Epic: Semantic search companion module (kbexplorer-search)

nodes.content:
• Separate @anokye-labs/kbexplorer-search npm package in a new repo.
  • Consumes KBNode/KBGraph/KBConfig types from kbexplorer-core (or inlined initially until kbexplorer-core is published).
  • Pluggable embedding providers (OpenAI, local models, configurable).
  • Checked-in artifacts are deterministic (sorted keys, no timestamps, content-hash keyed).
  • FAISS (via faiss-node or similar) as the default runtime index, but the design does not depend solely on a native binary index as the only source of truth.
  • Phased delivery: extraction → embedding → artifacts → query engine → CLI → service.
nodes.rawContent:
- Separate `@anokye-labs/kbexplorer-search` npm package in a new repo.
- Consumes `KBNode`/`KBGraph`/`KBConfig` types from kbexplorer-core (or inlined
  initially until kbexplorer-core is published).
- Pluggable embedding providers (OpenAI, local models, configurable).
- Checked-in artifacts are deterministic (sorted keys, no timestamps, content-hash keyed).
- FAISS (via faiss-node or similar) as the default runtime index, but the design does not
  depend solely on a native binary index as the only source of truth.
- Phased delivery: extraction → embedding → artifacts → query engine → CLI → service.

nodes.title: Success definition

nodes.content:
kbexplorer defines a structured knowledge graph: authored markdown nodes, frontmatter metadata, clusters, hierarchy, relationships, and source-aware content. This Epic creates a companion @anokye-labs/kbexplorer-search module that understands that model and turns it into a semantic search corpus — without making the visual graph app or the core CLI responsible for vector-search infrastructure.

The module has two complementary roles:

  1. Index production — reads the kbexplorer content model, derives searchable units from the graph (SearchUnits), generates embeddings via a pluggable provider, and writes checked-in search artifacts (embeddings, index metadata, node-to-vector mappings). These artifacts become part of the repository — they travel with branches, PRs, reviews, releases, and deployments.

  2. Index consumption — loads the checked-in artifacts, builds an efficient vector index (FAISS or similar), embeds incoming queries using the same configured model, and returns kbexplorer-native results: node IDs, titles, paths, clusters, snippets, scores, and graph-aware context.

The repository owns the semantic search corpus; the service only provides query execution. Embeddings and mapping files are durable, reviewable build outputs tied to the exact version of the kbexplorer graph.

nodes.title: What

nodes.content:
Search results should be graph-aware — they know node identity, cluster membership, hierarchy, authored connections, source citations, and page structure. A query for "how does audit validation work?" should return the relevant kbexplorer node, its relationship to nearby concepts, and enough metadata to place the result back into the graph. This makes semantic search feel native to kbexplorer rather than bolted on.

The design also fits the development workflow: a contributor changes content, runs the search index builder, commits both content and updated search artifacts. CI verifies artifact freshness. A hosted service deploys directly from repository state.

nodes.title: Evidence-based completion criteria

nodes.content:
Define and export the core type contracts in src/types.ts:

interface SearchUnit {
  nodeId: string;           // KBNode.id
  chunkIndex: number;       // 0 for single-chunk nodes
  text: string;             // searchable text content
  title: string;            // node title
  cluster: string;          // cluster id
  path?: string;            // source file path
  parentId?: string;        // hierarchy parent
  entityType?: string;      // structured node type
  identity?: string;        // canonical URN
  connections: string[];    // connected node IDs
  metadata: Record<string, unknown>; // extensible
}

interface EmbeddingVector {
  unitId: string;           // `${nodeId}#${chunkIndex}`
  vector: number[];         // embedding values
  model: string;            // model that produced this
  dimensions: number;
}

interface EmbeddingArtifact {
  version: number;
  generatedFrom: string;    // content hash of source graph
  model: string;
  dimensions: number;
  units: SearchUnit[];
  vectors: EmbeddingVector[];
}

interface SearchResult {
  nodeId: string;
  title: string;
  cluster: string;
  score: number;            // cosine similarity
  snippet: string;          // relevant text excerpt
  chunkIndex: number;
  path?: string;
  parentId?: string;
  identity?: string;
  entityType?: string;
  connections: string[];
  metadata: Record<string, unknown>;
}

interface SearchConfig {
  embedding: {
    provider: string;       // 'openai' | 'local' | 'custom'
    model: string;          // e.g. 'text-embedding-3-small'
    dimensions?: number;
    batchSize?: number;
  };
  artifacts: {
    dir: string;            // output directory for artifacts
  };
  chunking?: {
    maxTokens?: number;
    overlap?: number;
  };
}

interface EmbeddingProvider {
  name: string;
  embed(texts: string[]): Promise<number[][]>;
  dimensions: number;
}

Also inline a minimal subset of kbexplorer types (KBNode, KBEdge, KBGraph, Cluster, Connection) in src/kbexplorer-types.ts with a TODO to switch to @anokye-labs/kbexplorer-core when published.

nodes.title: Additional: Group by Edge Type

nodes.content: The Related panel should rank by edge weight × relevance, not just neighbor degree. A derived_from edge (weight 5.0) should rank higher than a mentions edge (weight 0.5), regardless of the target node's degree.

nodes.title: Expected

nodes.content:
The Related panel in the HUD shows the top 8 neighbors sorted by degree (connection count). This pushes out file nodes and other low-degree nodes, even when they have strong typed edges to the current node.

For example, content-pipeline has a derived_from edge (weight 3.0) to its source file file-content/content-pipeline.md and a references edge (weight 2.0) to file-src/engine/parser.ts — but neither appears in the Related panel because authored nodes with more connections rank higher by raw degree.

## Visual Identity System

### Icon Rendering
- Fluent icons sourced from `@fluentui/react-icons`, colored with their cluster color (not monochrome)
- Icons are drawn as SVG data URIs inside canvas shapes, with paths defined in `ICON_PATHS` (`nodeRenderer.ts`)

### Custom Node Shapes
- vis-network nodes use custom shapes via `ctxRenderer`: circles, rounded squares, and rounded rectangles
- Opaque node backgrounds prevent edges from showing through the node fill
- Disconnected nodes display a red **!** badge to flag orphan state

### Component Architecture
- `NodeVisual` component accepts a `clusterColor` prop for consistent color theming
- The 7 cluster surfaces still apply for UI chrome, but graph nodes bypass `NodeVisual` and use the custom canvas renderer directly

nodes.content:
The KB loader hook (src/hooks/useKnowledgeBase.ts) is the React hook that bootstraps the entire knowledge graph on app startup. It detects the content mode, fetches or loads data, and returns a discriminated union that the application shell uses to render loading, error, or ready states.

Mode Detection

The hook first calls detectLocalMode() from the local loader. If local mode is active (manifest exists), the entire graph loads from the pre-built manifest with zero API calls. Otherwise, it falls through to remote mode using the GitHub API.

export function useKnowledgeBase(sourceOverride?: SourceConfig): LoadingState {
  // 1. detectLocalMode() — check for manifest
  // 2. If local: loadLocalKnowledgeBase() — zero API calls
  // 3. If remote: loadConfig → loadRepoContent → loadAuthoredContent
  // 4. extractClusters → buildGraph → { graph, config }
}

Loading Pipeline (Remote Mode)

  1. loadConfig() — fetch config.yaml from the repo
  2. loadRepoContent() — fetch issues, tree, README via GitHub API
  3. loadAuthoredContent() — fetch markdown from content directory (optional)
  4. extractClusters() — derive clusters from all nodes via the parser
  5. buildGraph() — compute edges and related nodes via the graph engine

Error Handling

The hook catches all errors and maps them to user-friendly messages. Empty node arrays get specific messaging. The loading screen renders these messages.

Cancellation

The useEffect cleanup sets a cancelled flag, preventing state updates after unmount — avoiding React's "can't update unmounted component" warning during fast navigation. The type system and cache system provide the underlying data structures.
nodes.title: KB Loader Hook

nodes.content:
The keyboard navigation hook (src/hooks/useKeyboardNav.ts) adds global keyboard shortcuts to kbexplorer, making the entire knowledge graph navigable without a mouse. It was implemented as part of #16 and shipped in PR #8 alongside the theme system and HUD.

Active Shortcuts

Key Action Context
t Cycle theme (dark → light → sepia) Global
← Navigate to previous node Reading view
→ Navigate to next node Reading view

Implementation

The hook attaches a keydown listener to window and guards against input fields — shortcuts are suppressed when the user is typing in an INPUT, TEXTAREA, SELECT, or contentEditable element.

export function useKeyboardNav(
  graph: KBGraph | null,
  setTheme: (t: Theme) => void
): void {
  useEffect(() => {
    function handler(e: KeyboardEvent) {
      const tag = (e.target as HTMLElement)?.tagName;
      if (tag === 'INPUT' || tag === 'TEXTAREA') return;
      // Handle 't' for theme cycling, arrows for node navigation
    }
    window.addEventListener('keydown', handler);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('keydown', handler);
  }, [graph, setTheme]);
}

Node Sequence Navigation

Arrow keys navigate through the graph's node array in order. The hook reads the current node ID from window.location.hash, finds its index in graph.nodes, and navigates to the adjacent node. Navigation wraps around — pressing → on the last node goes to the first.

Theme Cycling

The t key reads the current theme from localStorage (via kbe-theme) and advances to the next mode using nextTheme() from the theme system. The responsive layout work (PR #18) ensured all views handle theme changes gracefully.

Integration

The application shell calls this hook with the loaded graph and the theme setter. The hook has no UI — it is purely behavioral.

The loading and error screens (src/components/LoadingScreen.tsx) provide feedback during the KB loader's async startup phase. These are the first things users see when opening kbexplorer, so they set the visual tone for the entire experience.

Loading State

While the KB loader hook fetches data from the GitHub API or loads the local manifest, the loading screen shows a Fluent Spinner component with a Body1 status message. The Fluent 2 refresh (PR #21) replaced the original custom spinner with the standard Fluent component.

Error State

If loading fails — typically due to GitHub API rate limiting (60 req/hour for unauthenticated requests) or missing GH_TOKEN in CI — the error screen displays the error message with recovery guidance. Common causes include rate limiting, empty manifests (fix: npm run prebuild), and missing tokens (fixed in PR #74, PR #75).

Integration

The application shell conditionally renders these screens based on the LoadingState discriminated union:

type LoadingState =
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'ready'; graph: KBGraph; config: KBConfig }
  | { status: 'error'; error: string };

The screens use Fluent tokens from the visual system and adapt to the active theme automatically.

The loading and error screens (`src/components/LoadingScreen.tsx`) provide feedback during the [KB loader](kb-loader)'s async startup phase. These are the first things users see when opening kbexplorer, so they set the visual tone for the entire experience.

## Loading State

While the [KB loader hook](kb-loader) fetches data from the [GitHub API](github-api) or loads the local manifest, the loading screen shows a Fluent `Spinner` component with a `Body1` status message. The Fluent 2 refresh ([PR #21](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/pull/21)) replaced the original custom spinner with the standard Fluent component.

## Error State

If loading fails — typically due to GitHub API rate limiting (60 req/hour for unauthenticated requests) or missing `GH_TOKEN` in CI — the error screen displays the error message with recovery guidance. Common causes include rate limiting, empty manifests (fix: `npm run prebuild`), and missing tokens (fixed in [PR #74](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/pull/74), [PR #75](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/pull/75)).

## Integration

The [application shell](app-shell) conditionally renders these screens based on the `LoadingState` discriminated union:

```typescript
type LoadingState =
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'ready'; graph: KBGraph; config: KBConfig }
  | { status: 'error'; error: string };
```

The screens use Fluent tokens from the [visual system](visual-system) and adapt to the active theme automatically.

nodes.content:
The local loader (src/engine/local-loader.ts) enables kbexplorer to run entirely offline by reading from a pre-built manifest instead of calling the GitHub API at runtime. This eliminates rate limiting, reduces startup latency, and makes the app work in CI environments — it was the central feature of the local mode initiative (#29–#37, delivered in PR #38).

Mode Detection

isLocalMode() checks the VITE_KB_LOCAL environment variable. detectLocalMode() is the async wrapper for hook compatibility. The KB loader hook calls detectLocalMode() first and branches accordingly — local mode means zero network calls.

export function isLocalMode(): boolean {
  return import.meta.env.VITE_KB_LOCAL === 'true';
}

The Manifest

The build scripts generate src/generated/repo-manifest.json at build time. This RepoManifest interface captures everything the API would have returned: configRaw, authoredContent (path→markdown map), tree (GHTreeItem array), readme, issues, pullRequests, commits, plus nodemapRaw and nodemapFiles for the node mapping system. The manifest script (#30) walks the file system and calls gh CLI for GitHub data.

Loading Pipeline

loadLocalKnowledgeBase() is the main entry point. It lazy-loads the manifest (cached in a module-level promise), builds a provider registry with authored, files, and work providers, then calls the orchestrator to run them in dependency order. The result is a { graph, config } pair identical to what the remote path produces.

The loader imports parseMarkdownFile, issueToNode, treeToNodes, extractClusters, buildGraph, and splitIntoSections from the parser and graph engine — the same functions used in remote mode, ensuring data consistency.

Glob Resolution

The loader includes a globToRegex() helper that converts simple glob patterns (like src/engine/*.ts) to regular expressions for matching against the manifest file tree. This supports the node mapping glob mode without requiring filesystem access at runtime.

Identity

All nodes loaded from the manifest receive identity URNs via assignIdentity(). Authored content gets urn:content:, files get urn:file:, issues get urn:issue:. The multi-layer identity system ties these together across providers.

Testing

The local data pipeline has comprehensive Vitest coverage (#37) including manifest generation, content parsing, and mode routing via the test suite.

The local loader (`src/engine/local-loader.ts`) enables kbexplorer to run entirely offline by reading from a pre-built manifest instead of calling the [GitHub API](github-api) at runtime. This eliminates rate limiting, reduces startup latency, and makes the app work in CI environments — it was the central feature of the local mode initiative ([#29–#37](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/issues/32), delivered in [PR #38](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/pull/38)).

## Mode Detection

`isLocalMode()` checks the `VITE_KB_LOCAL` environment variable. `detectLocalMode()` is the async wrapper for hook compatibility. The [KB loader hook](kb-loader) calls `detectLocalMode()` first and branches accordingly — local mode means zero network calls.

```typescript
export function isLocalMode(): boolean {
  return import.meta.env.VITE_KB_LOCAL === 'true';
}
```

## The Manifest

The [build scripts](build-scripts) generate `src/generated/repo-manifest.json` at build time. This `RepoManifest` interface captures everything the API would have returned: `configRaw`, `authoredContent` (path→markdown map), `tree` (GHTreeItem array), `readme`, `issues`, `pullRequests`, `commits`, plus `nodemapRaw` and `nodemapFiles` for the [node mapping](node-mapping) system. The manifest script ([#30](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/issues/30)) walks the file system and calls `gh` CLI for GitHub data.

## Loading Pipeline

`loadLocalKnowledgeBase()` is the main entry point. It lazy-loads the manifest (cached in a module-level promise), builds a [provider registry](providers-overview) with [authored](authored-provider), [files](files-provider), and [work](work-provider) providers, then calls the [orchestrator](orchestrator) to run them in dependency order. The result is a `{ graph, config }` pair identical to what the remote path produces.

The loader imports `parseMarkdownFile`, `issueToNode`, `treeToNodes`, `extractClusters`, `buildGraph`, and `splitIntoSections` from the [parser](parser) and [graph engine](graph-engine) — the same functions used in remote mode, ensuring data consistency.

## Glob Resolution

The loader includes a `globToRegex()` helper that converts simple glob patterns (like `src/engine/*.ts`) to regular expressions for matching against the manifest file tree. This supports the [node mapping](node-mapping) glob mode without requiring filesystem access at runtime.

## Identity

All nodes loaded from the manifest receive [identity](identity) URNs via `assignIdentity()`. Authored content gets `urn:content:`, files get `urn:file:`, issues get `urn:issue:`. The [multi-layer identity](multi-layer-identity) system ties these together across providers.

## Testing

The local data pipeline has comprehensive Vitest coverage ([#37](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/issues/37)) including manifest generation, content parsing, and mode routing via the [test suite](test-suite).

nodes.content:
The manifest generator (scripts/generate-manifest.js) is the pre-build script that creates the complete data snapshot used by the local loader. It replaces all runtime GitHub API calls with a single static JSON file.

What It Generates

src/generated/repo-manifest.json contains:

  1. File tree — GHTreeItem-compatible array from local file system walk
  2. Content files — all markdown from content/ directory, embedded as strings
  3. Issues — fetched via gh issue list CLI command
  4. Pull requests — fetched via gh pr list CLI command
  5. Commits — fetched via gh api for recent history
  6. Config — config.yaml and nodemap.yaml contents

Vite Integration

The Vite configuration includes a plugin that runs the manifest generator on buildStart (#35). This ensures freshness for both development and production builds.

npm run prebuild   # or: node scripts/generate-manifest.js

CI Lessons

Missing GH_TOKEN in CI silently produces empty work data. PR #74 fixed the deploy build, and PR #75 added required permissions. These failures were caught by Playwright E2E tests in the test suite.

Integration

The generator is called by the build scripts and feeds the local loader. The authored provider, files provider, and work provider all consume manifest data.

The manifest generator (`scripts/generate-manifest.js`) is the pre-build script that creates the complete data snapshot used by the [local loader](local-loader). It replaces all runtime [GitHub API](github-api) calls with a single static JSON file.

## What It Generates

`src/generated/repo-manifest.json` contains:

1. **File tree** — GHTreeItem-compatible array from local file system walk
2. **Content files** — all markdown from `content/` directory, embedded as strings
3. **Issues** — fetched via `gh issue list` CLI command
4. **Pull requests** — fetched via `gh pr list` CLI command
5. **Commits** — fetched via `gh api` for recent history
6. **Config** — `config.yaml` and `nodemap.yaml` contents

## Vite Integration

The [Vite configuration](vite-config) includes a plugin that runs the manifest generator on `buildStart` ([#35](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/issues/35)). This ensures freshness for both development and production builds.

```bash
npm run prebuild   # or: node scripts/generate-manifest.js
```

## CI Lessons

Missing `GH_TOKEN` in CI silently produces empty work data. [PR #74](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/pull/74) fixed the deploy build, and [PR #75](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/pull/75) added required permissions. These failures were caught by Playwright E2E tests in the [test suite](test-suite).

## Integration

The generator is called by the [build scripts](build-scripts) and feeds the [local loader](local-loader). The [authored provider](authored-provider), [files provider](files-provider), and [work provider](work-provider) all consume manifest data.

nodes.content:
The multi-layer identity specification defines how the same real-world entity maintains a stable identity across multiple graph layers and providers. Designed in #47 and implemented in commit 930f94c, this system prevents duplicate nodes and enables cross-layer navigation.

The Problem

A source file like src/engine/graph.ts can appear as: a file node from the files provider, a content node from the authored provider (as graph-engine), and a concept referenced in issues. Without identity, the graph engine treats these as separate nodes.

URN Scheme

The identity system assigns URN strings:

urn:file:src/engine/graph.ts   — file layer
urn:content:graph-engine        — content layer
urn:issue:42                    — work layer
urn:pr:76                       — work layer
urn:commit:930f94c              — work layer

Identity Linking

The file: field in nodemap.yaml entries creates identity links between content nodes and source files. The node mapping spec defines these mappings. buildIdentityIndex() groups nodes sharing a URN for merging.

Layer Model

The sense-making epic (#54) formalized four layers: File (from files provider), Content (from authored provider), Work (from work provider), and Concept (inferred). Identity URNs bridge these layers. The HUD layer toggles (#55) show/hide entire layers. The design decisions node explains the URN rationale.
nodes.rawContent:
The multi-layer identity specification defines how the same real-world entity maintains a stable identity across multiple graph layers and [providers](providers-overview). Designed in [#47](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/issues/47) and implemented in commit `930f94c`, this system prevents duplicate nodes and enables cross-layer navigation.

## The Problem

A source file like `src/engine/graph.ts` can appear as: a **file node** from the [files provider](files-provider), a **content node** from the [authored provider](authored-provider) (as `graph-engine`), and a **concept** referenced in issues. Without identity, the [graph engine](graph-engine) treats these as separate nodes.

## URN Scheme

The [identity system](identity) assigns URN strings:

```
urn:file:src/engine/graph.ts   — file layer
urn:content:graph-engine        — content layer
urn:issue:42                    — work layer
urn:pr:76                       — work layer
urn:commit:930f94c              — work layer
```

## Identity Linking

The `file:` field in `nodemap.yaml` entries creates identity links between content nodes and source files. The [node mapping spec](spec-node-mapping) defines these mappings. `buildIdentityIndex()` groups nodes sharing a URN for merging.

## Layer Model

The sense-making epic ([#54](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/issues/54)) formalized four layers: **File** (from [files provider](files-provider)), **Content** (from [authored provider](authored-provider)), **Work** (from [work provider](work-provider)), and **Concept** (inferred). Identity URNs bridge these layers. The [HUD](hud) layer toggles ([#55](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/issues/55)) show/hide entire layers. The [design decisions](design-decisions) node explains the URN rationale.

nodes.content:
The node mapping system (src/engine/nodemap.ts) defines how source files become graph nodes via the nodemap.yaml configuration file. This is the bridge between the raw repository file system and the curated knowledge graph — without it, the graph would either show every file (overwhelming) or require manual content authoring for each node (unscalable). It was designed in #41 and implemented in commit 611e138.

Five Processing Modes

Each nodemap.yaml entry specifies a mode that determines how files map to nodes:

  1. Single file — one file becomes one node (e.g., src/engine/graph.ts → graph-engine)
  2. Split — one file is split at ## headings into parent + section nodes via the parser's splitIntoSections()
  3. Merge — multiple files combine into a single node
  4. Glob — a pattern like src/engine/*.ts creates one node per matching file
  5. Directory — a directory listing becomes a navigable tree node
# nodemap.yaml example — single file mode
- id: graph-engine
  title: Graph Engine
  file: src/engine/graph.ts
  emoji: Flash
  cluster: engine
  connections: imports

Connection Derivation

After processing all entries, deriveConnections() makes a second pass to add edges. The connections field in each entry supports three strategies:

  • Explicit array — [graph-engine, parser] directly lists target node IDs
  • imports — extractImportPaths() parses import/require statements from source code, resolveImportPath() resolves relatives like ../types, and each match becomes an edge
  • references — scans content for inline links to other node IDs

I/O Abstraction

The module is standalone — callers provide readFile, listFiles, and listDirectory callbacks. This lets it work with both the GitHub API (remote mode) and the pre-built manifest (via the local loader) without any filesystem dependency.

Integration

The local loader and authored provider both call loadNodeMap() with raw YAML and I/O callbacks. The node mapping spec documents the full schema. The multi-layer identity system connects nodemap file entries to content nodes via urn:file: identity URNs in the identity system. The provider architecture (#40) uses node mapping as the foundation layer defined in the type system.

## Five Processing Modes

Each `nodemap.yaml` entry specifies a mode that determines how files map to nodes:

1. **Single file** — one file becomes one node (e.g., `src/engine/graph.ts` → `graph-engine`)
2. **Split** — one file is split at `##` headings into parent + section nodes via the [parser](parser)'s `splitIntoSections()`

4. **Glob** — a pattern like `src/engine/*.ts` creates one node per matching file
5. **Directory** — a directory listing becomes a navigable tree node

```yaml
# nodemap.yaml example — single file mode

  title: Graph Engine

  emoji: Flash
  cluster: engine
  connections: imports
```

## Connection Derivation

After processing all entries, `deriveConnections()` makes a second pass to add edges. The `connections` field in each entry supports three strategies:

- **Explicit array** — `[graph-engine, parser]` directly lists target node IDs
- **`imports`** — `extractImportPaths()` parses `import`/`require` statements from source code, `resolveImportPath()` resolves relatives like `../types`, and each match becomes an edge
- **`references`** — scans content for inline links to other node IDs

## I/O Abstraction

The module is standalone — callers provide `readFile`, `listFiles`, and `listDirectory` callbacks. This lets it work with both the [GitHub API](github-api) (remote mode) and the pre-built manifest (via the [local loader](local-loader)) without any filesystem dependency.

## Integration

The [local loader](local-loader) and [authored provider](authored-provider) both call `loadNodeMap()` with raw YAML and I/O callbacks. The [node mapping spec](spec-node-mapping) documents the full schema. The [multi-layer identity](multi-layer-identity) system connects nodemap file entries to content nodes via `urn:file:` identity URNs in the [identity system](identity). The provider architecture ([#40](https://github.com/anokye-labs/kbexplorer-template/issues/40)) uses node mapping as the foundation layer defined in the [type system](type-system).

nodes.content:
The node renderer (src/engine/nodeRenderer.ts) is the custom canvas drawing engine that paints every node in the constellation graph. Instead of using vis-network's built-in shapes, kbexplorer draws Fluent UI icons directly onto the HTML5 canvas — this gives pixel-perfect control over icon rendering, shape variants, and dark/light mode adaptation that the built-in shapes can't achieve.

How It Works

createNodeRenderer() returns a draw function that vis-network calls for each node on every frame:

function createNodeRenderer(
  iconName: string,   // Fluent icon name (e.g., "Flash", "Code")
  color: string,      // Cluster color hex
  size: number,       // Node radius in pixels
  isDark: boolean,    // Dark mode flag
  label?: string,     // Optional text label
  disconnected?: boolean
): (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, x: number, y: number) => void

The renderer paints a rounded shape (circle, rounded square, or rounded rectangle depending on icon type), fills it with the cluster color at reduced opacity, then draws the Fluent icon as an SVG data URI overlay. Labels render below the shape in the current theme's foreground color.

Shape System

The ICON_NODE_SHAPE map determines which shape each icon gets. The inferNodeShape() helper provides defaults — most icons render as circles, but document-related icons use rounded rectangles. This was part of the graph node shapes work in PR #28, which also added the overlay animation system.

Icon Library

The renderer embeds 150+ Fluent UI icon SVG paths in the ICON_PATHS dictionary — a subset of @fluentui/react-icons hand-selected for the knowledge graph use case. getIconImage() converts each icon to a canvas-drawable Image via SVG data URI construction and caches the result for performance. Icons are colored with their cluster color — never monochrome.

Dark Mode Rendering

In dark mode, background fills use lighter opacity and icon strokes invert. The isDark parameter flows from the theme system through the graph network factory. The hexToRgba() helper adjusts fill and stroke colors accordingly — without this, nodes would be invisible on dark backgrounds.

Integration

The renderer is consumed exclusively by the graph network factory's buildVisNode() function. Each node gets its own renderer instance, configured with the node's emoji and cluster color. The HUD minimap uses a simplified version for its smaller display. The visual system coordinates which icon surfaces use which rendering path.
